opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a huge relief. For a long time I just thought something was wrong with me as a person. I'd start ten things at once, get completely absorbed in something for hours, and then struggle to do a simple routine task. I'd forget small things, lose track of time, and I'd blame myself: "Why can't you just be disciplined like everyone else?"

When I started reading about ADHD and recognized so much of myself in it, it reframed everything. It wasn't that I was lazy or careless. My brain just works differently. It has a different relationship with attention, interest, and motivation. Once I understood that, I could stop fighting myself so hard and start designing my life around how I actually function.

It also helped me see the other side. The same thing that makes boring tasks painful is what lets me hyperfocus on a hard research problem for days, jump between ideas, and make connections other people might not. In research and building systems, that can be a real strength.

So now, instead of forcing myself into a mold, I build structure that works for me. I work with collaborators who complement me, I break things into pieces, and I lean into the work that energizes me. And I'm much kinder to myself. That self-acceptance was probably the biggest change, more than any productivity trick.

r001.rationale: She says recognizing herself in descriptions of ADHD reframed her experiences—such as difficulty with routine tasks and hyperfocus—as differences in how her brain works, rather than personal failings.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, for a long time I just thought I was lazy. Or undisciplined. I'd sit down to write a paper and three hours later I'd have twelve browser tabs open about something completely unrelated, and the paper would be two sentences long. And then I'd beat myself up about it, because everyone around me seemed to just... do the thing. Stanford, research, deadlines. People sat down and worked. I didn't understand why I couldn't.

So when I finally got the diagnosis, the first feeling wasn't relief, actually. It was something closer to grief. Like, oh, this was never a character flaw. All those years of calling myself names in my head, that wasn't fair. It was a brain that's wired to chase novelty and hyperfocus on whatever is most interesting right now, not whatever is most important.

But once I sat with it, it became incredibly freeing. Because now I had a model. I'm an engineer, I like models. If I know my attention is a resource that behaves a certain way, I can design around it. I stopped trying to force myself to be a morning person who does deep work for four hours straight. Instead I started leaning into the hyperfocus. When I'm locked in on something, I protect that time fiercely. And when I'm not, I don't fight it, I do the shallow stuff, the emails, the reviews.

I think a lot of what we call "making peace with yourself" is really just replacing judgment with curiosity. Instead of "why am I like this," it's "okay, I'm like this, what does that mean for how I should work?" That reframe changed everything. It even changed how I think about building tools. A lot of the projects I'm most excited about are, in some sense, me building scaffolding for a brain that doesn't naturally hold structure on its own. And it turns out a lot of other people needed that scaffolding too. They just weren't admitting it either.

r001.rationale: She says the diagnosis gave her a model for her attention and helped explain why she struggled to focus on tasks, reframing those experiences as brain wiring rather than a character flaw.

astra-6.text:
Learning about ADHD gave me a different way to understand myself. Things I’d interpreted as laziness or a lack of discipline became things I could approach with curiosity: Why is this difficult for me? What would actually help?

That didn’t mean I could suddenly explain everything, or that I no longer had to take responsibility. But I could take responsibility without constantly attacking myself. Instead of asking, “Why can’t I just try harder?” I could ask, “Can I change how I’m approaching this?”

For me, making peace with myself meant allowing those two things to coexist: I can want to grow, and I can be kinder to the person I am right now.

r001.rationale: She says learning about ADHD gave her a different way to understand herself and reframe experiences she had interpreted as laziness or lack of discipline.

sol-6.1.text:
Learning about ADHD gave me a different way to understand myself. Before, when I struggled to focus or follow through, I would turn it into a judgment about my character: Why am I so lazy? Why can’t I just do this? Having a framework helped me step back from that self-blame and ask, “What’s making this difficult, and what would actually help?”

It didn’t mean I stopped taking responsibility. It meant I could take responsibility without constantly attacking myself. For me, making peace with myself was letting go of the idea that I had to become a completely different person before I deserved some kindness.

r001.rationale: She says learning about ADHD gave her a different way to understand herself and helped explain earlier struggles with focus and follow-through.
